definition: Digression means a temporary departure from the main subject.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word digression. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know digression should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The planetarium show's single digression — ninety seconds on the smell of moon dust — was every kid's favorite part.
An aside is far slighter than a digression — one sentence long, a wink to the audience, then straight back to business, while a digression wanders for whole minutes before finding its way home.
A derailment goes further than a digression — a digression steps off the path meaning to return; a derailment never finds the track again.

A tangent is the casual word for the same wander off the subject, and it makes no promise about coming home — speakers fly off on tangents and often stay gone. A digression is the rounder trip: a temporary departure that means to return to the subject, and does.

A sidetrack is what the wander does to you — you get sidetracked, tugged briefly off your task or your point by something more interesting. A digression is the departure itself, taken on purpose by a speaker or writer who means, all along, to come back.

The bride's family times him now; the record digression is seven minutes, round trip.
Digression is the exact word for those wanders, because a digression is a temporary departure from the main subject — and the key word is temporary: he leaves the story and he comes back to it.
Circumlocution never leaves the subject at all; it circles the point without touching it.
A digression at least goes somewhere, just not where the story was going.
Digression suits essays, lectures, and long dinners — departures that mean to return.

Okafor's history class remembers the map of Constantinople -- and the day he stopped mid-sentence to talk about his grandmother's spice cabinet.
It sounded like a lost cause.
For six or seven minutes he described cinnamon arriving by caravan, the smell of the tin she kept it in, the price a cook once paid for cloves.
Then, without a pause, he tapped the map: every one of those spices had passed through this one city, which was why three empires had fought for it.
The digression, the class realized, had never truly left the subject; it had been circling it the whole time.
Years later, his students compared notes and found the pattern held: however far the story wandered, it landed back on the lesson, and the lesson stuck because of the trip.
